#2367. Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1659 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you?
  • Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell.
  • It has been revealed that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

It has been revealed that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

This being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

In a recent development, viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

Sources indicate that after sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a newly introduced variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

It has been revealed that then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

Industry observers note that that vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

Industry observers note that drusilla is one of the new characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a massive chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

Industry observers note that thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace rapidly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

It has been revealed that leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

Sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating latest version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

According to recent reports, no spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

But while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.).

Throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up says "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

It has been revealed that it's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.).

Anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. (At least, until Collins decides to return to Panem.).

Sources indicate that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters Nov. 20.

#2366. Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1312 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard.
  • In a recent development, by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release.
  • So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard. If you're not playing it but are reading this, we can guess why.

In a recent development, by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release. If that's the case, you're going to miss out on the biggest gaming launch of the year — and possibly all time. FOMO is a natural human reaction to these sorts of things, and here at Mashable, we fully understand the pain of not being sure whether or not you should buy a console just for GTA 6.

So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.

The primary and most obvious reason to buy a console for GTA 6 is that it's the only real way to play it at launch. There is technically another way that we'll cover in a little while, but for all intents and purposes, you cannot have the same experience everyone else is having without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series console.

By all accounts, GTA 6 is a pretty fantastic video game. You probably wouldn't want to miss out on that. What are you going to do while everyone else is having an amazing time parading through Leonida, read books? Come on, that sounds boring.

It has been revealed that one thing that's also worth remembering is that other video games exist. A lot of them, in fact. If you buy a PS5 or Xbox Series console, you'll have access to the last six years of current-gen releases, some of which are extremely good. They might even be better than GTA 6! As a fun bonus, through the magic of backward compatibility, ports, remasters, and remakes, you'll also be able to play countless video games from previous generations of hardware, too.

Lastly, both consoles (at least the models with disc drives) work as 4K Blu-ray players, if you're into collecting physical versions of movies. That's cool, too.

Both consoles have been hard to find in stock (thanks in large part to GTA 6), but the Xbox Series S and PS5 Digital Edition are both in stock at Amazon, as of this writing. If you're not sure whether to buy a PS5 or the Xbox Series X/S, keep scrolling for a breakdown of the pros and cons.

First, foremost, in the biggest, boldest font you can imagine: You shouldn't buy a console just for GTA 6 because they're stupid expensive these days.

Recent findings suggest that both Xbox and PlayStation have recently increased the prices of their consoles due to real-world economic concerns. The cheapest model right now is a $499 Xbox Series S, and Rockstar hasn't shown us that version of the game yet, leading to speculation that the game is better on PS5, which starts at $599. If you want the best possible version at launch, you'll need a PS5 Pro, which costs $899 — and is currently out of stock at most retailers.

In other words, there just isn't a particularly affordable way to play GTA 6 traditionally at launch, unless you already own the hardware.

Sources indicate that there are, of course, other reasons to not get a console for GTA 6. There exists a slim likelihood that you won't like the game, though so far, most people who have played it have come away with positive impressions. It also won't have an online component at launch, and no one knows when it will get one. For a lot of people, GTA Online is the only GTA experience that matters, and that audience will have very little to do in the new game until some nebulous point in the future when Rockstar decides to cater to them.

Recent findings suggest that maybe you just don't care that much about non-GTA video games, either. If that's the case, it's hard to recommend spending this much money on a box that will only play one game.

There was a lot of anxiety on the internet prior to the game's launch surrounding the potential differences between the different console versions. The good news is that the game is out and has been fully tested by experts, and the verdict is that you almost can't go wrong with GTA 6 on any platform.

Recent findings suggest that digital Foundry is an outlet and YouTube channel that offers expert-level tech analysis of games, and they have a fairly comprehensive guide to the different console versions of GTA 6. According to DF, both the PS5 and Series X versions run at the same resolution and target the same frame rate, with some performance dips on both in more intense sequences. In other words, the base PS5 and Series X versions are roughly the same, though the PS5's controller does have exclusive haptic feedback features for gameplay like driving cars.

There is also the matter of the PS5 Pro and Xbox Series S consoles, though. DF notes the PS5 Pro is the best version of the game, with a sharper resolution and higher-quality shadows to go along with smoother performance. That was to be expected. Sadly, it sounds like the Series S version is probably the least desirable build of the game. Its visuals have been marginally downgraded with a lower resolution and some reduced visual settings, but more importantly, DF's analysis found that the frame rate can dip below 20fps in extreme circumstances.

We do have good news for Xbox Series S gamers, however. Mashable Editorial Director Eric Miller has played the game on Series S and has had a positive first impression so far. If you have no other way to play GTA 6, it should work, but it will be reduced in quality compared to the others.

There is technically a way to play GTA 6 without buying a newly introduced PS5 or Xbox, but it's not a viable alternative for most people.

According to recent reports, to be clear, there are multiple massive reasons why you might not want to do this. For starters, it involves a monthly subscription. Beyond that, Microsoft recently imposed strict monthly hour limits on Cloud Gaming. With this system, you will be able to play at most 15 hours of GTA 6 per month. Many people are going to play more than that in the first weekend it's out. Even if those aren't concerns, game streaming is subject to the limits of your home internet, meaning that latency and buffering can and will occur. That version of the game will also be visually downgraded to some degree, per Rockstar.

Industry observers note that if game streaming (understandably) doesn't work for you, the last option is to wait for the PC version. Unfortunately, Rockstar has not said anything about when GTA 6 will launch on PC, though a recent report pegged it as coming in early 2027. That will likely be the best version of the game in terms of visuals, but only if you have the requisite hardware. For those who already have capable gaming PCs, this might be the best option for playing GTA 6, provided you're patient enough to wait. For those who don't, this is going to be even more expensive than buying a console, so maybe don't bother.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time, Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi are all fighting on the exact same turf: wider, passport-style book foldables built to feel natural both closed and open.
  • Both the iPhone Duo and the standard Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 rely on dual-camera systems – a primary wide sensor paired with an ultrawide – leaving every zoom step past 1x to sensor crops and computational upscaling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time, Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi are all fighting on the exact same turf: wider, passport-style book foldables built to feel natural both closed and open. In theory, that levels the ergonomic playing field. Once you open the camera apps, though, three wildly different hardware philosophies emerge.

Both the iPhone Duo and the standard Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 rely on dual-camera systems – a primary wide sensor paired with an ultrawide – leaving every zoom step past 1x to sensor crops and computational upscaling. Meanwhile, the Xiaomi 18 Fold squeezes a full Leica-engineered triple-camera array into its sleek frame, anchored by a 200MP main camera and a dedicated 50MP 3.3x optical periscope telephoto.

Sources indicate that before the iPhone Duo launched, much of the criticism focused on Apple dropping the telephoto lens compared to its flagship Pro range. Samsung was rightly lambasted for the same compromise just a few months earlier, but can a passport-size foldable actually offer it all?

To judge this and see how those hardware choices hold up in the real world, I took all three foldables around Dubai Marina from harsh midday sun through sunset, blue hour, and neon-lit nights.

Here is how they actually compare, starting with the specs on paper.

50MP, 80mm equivf/2.8, OIS3.5x optical zoom.

It's hard for a modern smartphone camera to take bad photos in good lighting, and all three foldables capture crisp, share-worthy photos. Yet each phone immediately reveals a distinct personality, starting with framing.

Both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Xiaomi 18 Fold shoot at a wider 23mm focal length, while the iPhone Duo’s 26mm main lens crops noticeably tighter into every scene.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

The Ocean Empress yacht along the marina is a textbook showcase of how these three pipelines diverge.

Xiaomi’s Leica Vibrant profile produces the most inviting, rich-looking photo straight out of the camera, giving the red-mahogany hull and gold latticework warm depth without blowing out the silver skyscrapers behind it.

Samsung favors cooler tones and aggressive contrast, leaving the lower-left hull signage significantly darker, while Apple prioritizes balanced exposure across the entire frame.

Push dynamic range to the limit—like shooting from underneath a massive concrete bridge out into harsh midday sun—and the iPhone Duo’s computational HDR takes the lead.

Recent findings suggest that apple renders the shaded underside of the concrete arch smoothly and keeps the lower boat deck legible, trading away a bit of blue saturation in the bright sky. Samsung keeps the sky bluest, but crushes the bridge overhang into a flat, greenish-grey shadow. Xiaomi sits comfortably in the middle, holding better sky color than Apple while avoiding Samsung’s crushed shadows.

It has been revealed that switch to the ultrawide lenses, and we see further subtle differences, largely due to hardware choices. While Samsung (13mm, 0.5x) and Apple (14mm, 0.6x) deliver true sweeping ultrawide perspectives, the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s 17mm (0.7x) ultrawide is noticeably narrower – and slower at f/2.4, which impacts the amount of light it can capture.

Standing in front of Pier 7, that 4mm focal-length gap between Samsung and Xiaomi is dramatic: the Galaxy Z Fold 8 captures the entire skyscraper on the far left edge, whereas the Xiaomi 18 Fold slices it clean out of the frame.

Between the two wider shooters, Samsung gives you slightly more real estate and bolder blue skies, while the iPhone Duo handles harsh architectural reflections on the sunlit right-hand tower and deep shadows under the skybridge with noticeably better dynamic range.

If you care about zoom on a foldable, or you're actively considering these three devices, this is the entire ballgame.

According to recent reports, neither the iPhone Duo nor the standard Galaxy Z Fold 8 includes an optical telephoto lens, leaving both reliant on main-sensor digital crops. Do you actually need a dedicated telephoto lens, though?

According to recent reports, the Xiaomi 18 Fold packs a native 80mm (3.3x) periscope telephoto – and it embarrasses the competition from 3x all the way out to 96x. Look no further: this is the passport-style foldable made for an actual pro camera experience.

Recent findings suggest that at 2x (46mm–52mm), all three phones lean on high-resolution main-sensor crops and look sharp enough for social media. Push past 3x, however, and the gap opens immediately.

In front of La Brasseria, the iPhone Duo actually outshoots the Galaxy Z Fold 8 at ~4x: even though Apple crops tighter to 4.5x (107mm) compared to Samsung’s 3.8x (92mm), the iPhone’s 48MP sensor crop resolves cleaner lettering on the red menu banners and crisper horizontal slats behind the sign, whereas Samsung’s denoising smears the striped awning into watercolor mush.

Then you switch to the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s 3.3x (80mm) periscope – and neither digital crop comes close. Real glass resolves individual threads in the awning fabric, crisp white diamond motifs, and clean metallic edges on the sign, staying remarkably sharp even pushed to 6.7x (160mm) and 9.6x (230mm).

Pushing to maximum range across the Marina skyline reveals an interesting reversal between Apple and Samsung at ~10x.

While Apple won at ~4x, its 11x (263mm) ceiling turns soft and muddy on the distant Grosvenor House spire, while Samsung’s 9.6x (230mm) AI reconstruction sharpens straight architectural lines, keeping the GH monogram and pyramidal latticework distinct.

Still, Xiaomi’s 9.6x (230mm) periscope shot easily beats both with natural, optical-grade clarity – and then keeps going to 29x (690mm), 58x (1380mm), and an outrageous 96x (2300mm), pulling usable detail out of a rooftop emblem that is barely a speck at 1x.

Once the sun drops over Dubai Marina, metering strategy becomes just as notable as sensor size – and Samsung’s auto-exposure makes some puzzling choices.

According to recent reports, at night, Xiaomi and Apple trade blows on the primary lenses, depending on your taste. Dropping to 1/20s lets the Xiaomi 18 Fold hold sensitivity down at ISO 400, capturing a wide 23mm frame with rich contrast, deep water reflections, and well-tamed storefront screens.

The iPhone Duo (1/25s, ISO 500) lifts shadows more aggressively across the sandstone towers and walkway with virtually zero noise, though its tighter 26mm lens clips the right edge. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 inexplicably fires at 1/98s and pushes sensitivity to ISO 2500, resulting in darker shadows and visible grain on close inspection.

This is a fairly common occurrence in Samsung smartphones, and I hope we'll see it addressed in upcoming launches.

Zooming in at night completely flips the daytime hierarchy between Apple and Samsung.

Looking down at the glowing teardrop lanterns in the plaza, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 clips the lanterns into blown-out white blobs at 1.9x and 3.8x, and when it finally tames the highlights at 9.6x (230mm), heavy noise reduction smears the pedestrians and cafe tables into a soft painting.

Industry observers note that by contrast, the iPhone Duo’s multi-frame HDR keeps the intricate geometric lattice inside every lantern crisp at 4.5x (107mm) and even 11x (263mm). Still, the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s dedicated 3.3x–9.6x periscope wins easily, resolving cleaner filigree, flowerbeds, and paving tiles than either digital crop.

Challenging indoor venues – dim lounges, heavy colored LEDs, and high-contrast backlit signage – expose how each brand handles mixed white balance and bright light sources.

In a recent development, in a dimly lit lounge corner, Apple and Samsung prioritize highlight protection: both keep the white neon script ("We dont fit in either") sharp and legible while preserving rich color in the hanging fringe lampshades. Xiaomi takes the opposite approach, pushing 1/25s and ISO 1600 to illuminate dark velvet curtains and doorways that disappear into shadow on the others, though the neon tubing blooms noticeably more.

Flood a room in monochromatic red lighting, however, and Xiaomi’s color science shines. The Xiaomi 18 Fold (ISO 500) holds true, deep crimson across the ceiling ductwork and light pillars while keeping the floor and booths clean. The iPhone Duo stays close in color accuracy (aside from motion blur on a passing guest at 1/20s), whereas the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (ISO 1250) shifts the red LEDs noticeably toward hot pink and magenta.

Similarly, facing the heavily backlit CARGO reception wall, Xiaomi wins on both framing and dynamic range – keeping the full "SINCE 2014" wall lettering intact on the left (which Apple’s 26mm lens crops off) while controlling the orange-white halo glow around the block letters with the cleanest shadow detail.

All three phones handle a tricky portrait cutout along the Marina promenade – cleanly separating the triangular gap inside a bent arm resting on the metal railing without accidentally blurring the bar itself.

Xiaomi takes the crown with creamy, optical-looking Leica bokeh and warm, flattering skin tones against the sunlit towers. The iPhone Duo is a close second, lifting facial shadows slightly brighter in a tighter 26mm crop, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 applies more conservative background blur – offset somewhat if you enjoy Samsung’s signature Color Point monochrome-background effect.

Color Point is my favorite portrait mode feature on any device, and it's available on all Samsung phones, making it particularly useful regardless of the Galaxy hardware you buy.

In a recent development, one of the key benefits companies promote for buying a foldable is its form factor and its ability to use the rear cameras to take selfies. This is also used to argue that foldables don't need the best selfie-camera hardware, or, in the case of the iPhone Duo, can use under-display cameras.

Take this final comparison with a grain of salt, as it wasn’t the most scientific test. Still, it highlighted two practical realities of shooting selfies on foldables.

First, on the cover cameras, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 wins two-person selfies effortlessly: its wider 23mm lens fits both people comfortably, handles harsh overhead sunlight without washing out, and keeps both faces sharp.

In a recent development, the Xiaomi 18 Fold keeps both people in focus too, but suffers from heavy backlight flare when the sun sits behind your shoulder. Worst of all, the iPhone Duo crops tight at 28mm and falls straight into Apple’s single-subject portrait trap – keeping me sharp while completely blurring out my mom standing just inches behind me.

It has been revealed that second, if you want to bypass those f/2.2 cover sensors and use the much better rear cameras for selfies, Apple makes the experience unnecessarily frustrating. Unlike Samsung and Xiaomi – which put full camera controls right on the cover screen and let you trigger a timer simply by showing your palm – the iPhone Duo gives you no on-screen controls on the outer display and no palm gesture. Trying to awkwardly grip an unfolded foldable one-handed while stretching your fingers to press the Camera Control button or volume keys almost guarantees camera shake.

It's unlikely a single phone wins in every part of this comparison, so which phone wins overall? Here's how they ranked overall.

In a recent development, these results won't come as a huge surprise. While Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi have all converged on wide, passport-style foldables, their camera hardware choices split them decisively in real-world shooting.

Xiaomi 18 Fold proves that foldables need a telephoto.

By opting for a dedicated telephoto lens and offering considerably better all-around hardware, the Xiaomi 18 Fold proves that a slim passport-style foldable can deliver a pro-like camera.

According to recent reports, the iPhone Duo takes a solid second place due to reliable point-and-shoot HDR, strong ultrawide performance, and cleaner night highlight retention than Samsung. As for Samsung, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 wins a couple of categories, but overall, it still has work to do to keep pace with its rivals.

Breaking: Everything about BepiColombo entering Mercury orbit on Saturday

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A robotic spacecraft that has spent eight years looping around the inner solar system is finally set to lock into orbit around Mercury, the planet closest to the sun.
  • In a recent development, the European-Japanese mission, called BepiColombo, carries two science probes stacked on top of each other.
  • According to recent reports, A big engine burn should steer the pair into a regular, closed orbit that passes over the planet's north and south poles on Saturday, Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A robotic spacecraft that has spent eight years looping around the inner solar system is finally set to lock into orbit around Mercury, the planet closest to the sun.

In a recent development, the European-Japanese mission, called BepiColombo, carries two science probes stacked on top of each other. One is the European Space Agency's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO. The other is Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, nicknamed Mio.

According to recent reports, A big engine burn should steer the pair into a regular, closed orbit that passes over the planet's north and south poles on Saturday, Nov. 21.

Mercury is the least explored planet in the inner solar system. Only two spacecraft have ever visited it, NASA's Mariner 10 in the 1970s and Messenger in the 2010s. That will make BepiColombo just the second mission to orbit Mercury and the first to put two orbiters there at once. One probe will observe the planet itself and the other will study its space environment. Scientists hope the results will show how rocky planets like Earth form and change when they're born close to their star.

Reaching Mercury is actually harder than getting to Pluto. Falling toward the sun isn't the only problem. It's bleeding off enough energy to avoid overshooting the planet.

BepiColombo released on Oct. 20, 2018, on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. For most of the trip, it rode on a separate engine module that used ion thrusters. These engines push the spacecraft by firing charged particles out the back. The force was about as strong as the weight of two sheets of paper resting on your hand. But the thrusters ran for two years, carrying the spacecraft about 6 billion miles.

According to recent reports, the spacecraft also used gravity from nearby planets to bend its path. It swung past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times. In Sep. 2024, it passed within about 100 miles of Mercury, the closest any spacecraft has ever flown past a planet. The trip wasn't smooth sailing. The engine module's solar panels started losing power, so the team had to slow down and push back the arrival date. Controllers detached the engine module on Sep. 3.

"It's a very difficult mission and very challenging because we are flying into a very, very harsh environment," Bruno Sousa, ESA's head of operations definition and engineering, noted during a livestream that day. Mercury's surface can drop below -290 degrees Fahrenheit at night and climb above 750 degrees during the day. The spacecraft gets baked from two sides — by sunlight and heat rising off the planet.

Sources indicate that the arrival itself is unusual. Most missions hit the brakes hard and drop straight into orbit. BepiColombo is coming in slowly instead, and it gets there in steps. First, it drifts into Mercury's gravitational grip on a loose, irregular path that doesn't loop all the way around the planet. Engineers call this "weak capture." Spacecraft operations manager Ignacio "Nacho" Clérigo noted no one has tried it with a planet before, only with moons. Saturday's major burn swaps that wandering path for a true orbit. It starts out as a long, lopsided oval, and the spacecraft fires its engines about every three days to reel it in.

Sources indicate that as the orbit tightens, a series of handoffs follow. On Dec. 9 and 10, the European orbiter releases Mio into its final orbit. Full science work should begin in April 2027.

Mercury holds plenty of puzzles. It's unusually heavy for its size. Apart from Earth, it's the only rocky planet with a magnetic field surrounding the whole planet. Scientists want to learn whether Mercury's huge liquid core has a solid center. Others proposal to measure magnesium, potassium, and calcium in the space around Mercury. Those elements offer indirect clues about what the surface is made of.

The mission is named for Italian mathematician and engineer Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo. His work on using planets' gravity to steer spacecraft helped make the earlier Mercury missions possible as well as BepiColombo's long, looping route.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

It has been revealed that "We have to be really careful about what we're claiming that video games can actually do for us," Grines said. It's useful when individuals are exposed to behaviors that are typically associated with relationship satisfaction as a whole — like spending time together — but, she said, "your girlfriend doesn't have a meter on her forehead that increased the more you...show her attention.".

In a recent development, part of the online conversation stems from the relationship between GTA 6 protagonists Jason and Lucia, whose connection develops through the player's actions. While players can choose to keep their relationship platonic, the game still tracks their bond. Holding hands, buying flowers, giving compliments, sending texts, and running errands together (which may or may not involve committing crimes) can all improve their relationship score.

The relationship meter gives players a sense of where Jason and Lucia stand with one another, Mashable's editorial director Eric Miller explained to me, a self-professed non-gamer. While previous GTA games have featured romantic relationships and family dynamics, GTA 6 takes things a step further by allowing players to actively shape the protagonists' relationship. Depending on their actions, Jason and Lucia can be running on empty (1/4), partners in crime (2/4), crazy in love (3/4), or hot together (4/4).

According to recent reports, grines is skeptical that simply performing these actions in a game can teach emotional intelligence. "You're literally playing a game when you could be participating in your relationship," Grines continued. That's another line of thinking that's echoed on social media today: That people (mostly men) are doing chores for Lucia instead of their IRL girlfriend.

One of Grines' clients told her that his girlfriend isn't letting him buy the game — but not because of Lucia. It's actually because of the strip club scenes and how realistic the characters look. The girlfriend isn't comfortable with him going to strip clubs in real life, so why would she be comfortable with him going to one in a video game? As in our discussion over whether playing GTA 6 is cheating, Grines noted she's entitled to set a boundary.

Real relationships, of course, are more complicated than any in-game relationship meter can capture. And Grines warns against having unrealistic expectations for how video games can improve romance. While seeing a healthy relationship modeled in front of you can be useful, she mentioned that modeling doesn't always create behavioral change. Being a good boyfriend in the game doesn't factor in a real partner's own preferences, emotions, and agency. (For example, your real girlfriend may hate flowers!).

That doesn't mean GTA 6 can't bring couples closer together. Gaming can be a shared experience, as PCMag's Jordan Minor demonstrated when he played the game with his wife.

Industry observers note that "It's great that people can experiment and they can repeat actions that may improve their relationship satisfaction," she said. "The real test will be if they can take it out of the video game and into their real lives.".

It has been revealed that not everyone likes this element of the game. Right-wing (or right-wing adjacent) influencers Asmongold and Clavicular (who was indicted on two rape charges yesterday) expressed their distaste for GTA 6. The former called the game a "cuck simulator" while playing it on stream, and Clavicular said the game is "insanely cucked.".

Then again, GTA 6 is the highest-rated game of all time, so the haters are in the minority.

It has been revealed that motorola went all-in on premium this year with the Signature 27. While many consumers eagerly awaited this phone, some won't see it at its full potential.

Certain specs must be met before companies (or rather, consumers) can slap a premium label on a phone. The Motorola Signature 27 focuses on key areas: its display, camera, chipset, and battery. It's the latter—its battery—that's come under scrutiny in one market. According to Android Authority, the Motorola Signature 27's battery will suffer a hit overseas.

Reports have conflicted with the Signature 27's original 7,000mAh battery announcement. The publication highlighted this, then reached out to Motorola for clarification. A spokesperson responded, stating the device "will feature a different battery configuration in Germany." As a result, it looks like German consumers will find the Signature 27 with a 5,500mAh cell, not 7,000mAh.

This is a sharp 1,500mAh drop, but Motorola claims it had no choice.

In its statement, Motorola told the publication that it had to drop the phone's battery to "comply with local regulatory requirements related to lithium batteries." The report adds that this huge battery cut is worth roughly 17 hours of battery time (~61 hours vs 77 hours).

In a recent development, strangely, a report claimed U.K. consumers might've suffered from this battery cut, too. Apparently, the Signature 27 was listed with a 5,500mAh battery; however, it's reportedly since been updated to the higher figure.

It's unclear how this might affect German consumers who were interested in the Signature 27. The battery (right now) is the only aspect of the phone that's suffering from country-specific regulations. During launch, the phone was declared with an incredibly bright 6.8-inch Extreme AMOLED Duo display with 12,000 nits. Motorola stuck to its premium promise and delivered Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 SoC (a first for the brand).

For mobile gamers, the firm integrated its ArcticMesh cooling system, increasing its size by 40% to help keep temperatures lower during longer sessions.

Would something like this matter to you? A reduction from 7,000mAh to 5,500 mAh, I mean.

Here's why I ask—and I'll play both sides here. Motorola wanted to release a phone that firmly leaned into "premium." One could say it did. However, if you look at Samsung and its Galaxy S26 Ultra (S25 Ultra... S24 Ultra...), it features a 5,000mAh battery. The Korean OEM has kept this exact same 5,000mAh cell for a while, and yet it's still premium. Premium tag, premium price, everything. Of course, Motorola's sharp reduction will cut down how long users can keep scrolling, but it's still more than Samsung's latest Ultra.

#2353. This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’

This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that at 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote.
  • In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort.
  • It has been revealed that his startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a upcoming class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

It has been revealed that his startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a upcoming class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”.

In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.

Recent findings suggest that “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” notes Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”.

It has been revealed that dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”.

As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance tech giant, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.

Recent findings suggest that early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.

In a recent development, when Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

It has been revealed that around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, newly introduced defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.

“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says.

To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.

Sources indicate that in April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.

Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” indicates Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”.

It has been revealed that seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he indicates. “No one had ever seen that before.”.

When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he stated.

In a recent development, the week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” states Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the tech giant would be to part ways and focus on different things.”.

By the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.

Industry observers note that YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”.

Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.

“You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” indicates Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”.

But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” indicates Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”.

According to recent reports, so far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.

Recent findings suggest that if he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these latest missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?

In a recent development, dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these challenges. He indicates he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.

By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global problem. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he notes. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”.

But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

According to recent reports, mcKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, launched a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile organization invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.

Sources indicate that “I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he says. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”.

Polemos Industries unveiled itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.

According to recent reports, the video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first manufacturer. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.

In a recent development, dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he notes. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”.

Tech Report: ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Is a Perfect Game. Rushing Through It Would Be a Mistake

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hey, maybe don’t just immediately go to the strip club.
  • The biggest video game ever has turned out to be one of the very best.
  • In a recent development, I’ve spent a few hours in the game, and one thing becomes clear right away: This game is a slow burn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hey, maybe don’t just immediately go to the strip club. Look, I know that’s what you want to do right away when you start Grand Theft Auto VI. This is a GTA game after all—that sort of outlet for titillation is a common theme in this franchise. But going straight to the good stuff isn’t the best way to play this game.

The biggest video game ever has turned out to be one of the very best. With near-universally perfect review scores, GTA VI has emerged as an absolute behemoth that has lived up to 13 years of hype.

In a recent development, I’ve spent a few hours in the game, and one thing becomes clear right away: This game is a slow burn. The GTA franchise has always been high-octane, arcade-style, prioritizing hyperviolence and exaggerated physics that let your character go wild in the digital sandbox. But the latest installation is much more reserved. Vehicles and player movements feel heavier. The characters have deeper, more emotional backstories and motivations. The world has more interactivity and reacts to your actions in much more varied ways.

It evokes a play style that feels very much in common with Rockstar’s previous title, Red Dead Redemption 2. It was a Western that made the player feel the friction of an often slow, plodding life that didn’t shy away from simulating all the chores of a horse-bound cowboy in the 1800s. GTA VI, set in the modern era, is faster-paced but still carries that intentionality to slow the player down.

That manifests in ways that might feel like busywork. Instead of having access to all your weapons and outfits, you have to make space for the things you want to bring with you and store everything else in the back of your car. You have to call someone to fix your car and wait for them to arrive. Yeah, you have to paint your house and buy your girlfriend flowers. Get used to it. This can sometimes feel like a chore, but it slows the player down to give them time to examine the world around them.

Once you start looking around and really take everything in, the level of detail is truly unique. Leonida—GTA VI’s mirror version of Miami, Florida—is so varied and splendid it is almost overwhelming. After the game’s on-the-rails introductory missions open up into the first opportunity for an open-world sojourn, the sheer scale of this world becomes apparent. Zooming out on the map and seeing the vast expanse of unexplored territory is dizzying.

Sources indicate that there is just so much Leonida, and none of it feels sparse or unfinished. Every place, person, animal, and environmental asset feels fully fleshed out. Driving down the road, with other cars zooming past, is photorealistic enough to look nearly like real dash-cam footage. This game, as I have muttered to myself over and over again while playing, “is simply insane.”.

In a recent development, if you’ve followed the GTA VI saga, this likely won’t surprise you. Developer Rockstar and its parent organization Take-Two have spent around a billion dollars to develop the game. It’s taken 13 years. The company even delayed the game multiple times to make sure it was polished.

It has been revealed that there is massive hype, and at this point I’d say what Rockstar has achieved here has surpassed that hype. The game is likely to be the pinnacle of this era of video games, the final grand blockbuster achieved without the use of generative AI.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been playing GTA games for a long time. I’ll probably be playing this one for the rest of my life. Like me, you’re probably very excited to dive into this gigantic world. The best way to do that is not to try to see it all at once. Pace yourself. Look out for the small moments, as they may lead to something more profound than you’re expecting. Slow down, and you can really feel how the world reacts.

According to recent reports, nothing else like this game exists. And there probably won’t be for a very long time. Might as well make it last.

There's never a convenient time for your car to break down, but a freezing winter morning when you're already running late for work has to be among the worst possible scenarios.

Thankfully, modern automotive technology has made it a lot easier to understand what's going on with your vehicle, often without specialist knowledge or an expensive trip to the repair shop.

Tools once reserved for professional workshops can now connect directly to your smartphone and provide useful information about your car's condition through easy-to-use apps.

TOPDON is one of the companies making this technology more accessible, and offers everything from affordable Bluetooth diagnostic scanners to advanced equipment designed for professional mechanics.

This Black Friday, the tech giant is launching a substantial sale across its automotive range, with promotional prices running from November 19 through November 30.

One of the simplest ways to prepare for winter is to make sure your car's battery is in good condition before temperatures drop.

The TOPDON BT100 Battery Tester, available for $43.99 during Black Friday, provides a straightforward way to check the condition of a 12V battery without visiting a garage.

It can assess battery health and starting performance to help drivers determine whether a battery might need attention before it leaves them stranded.

Of course, even a well-maintained vehicle can experience an unexpected flat battery, which is why keeping a portable jump starter in the trunk is a sensible precaution.

The TOPDON JS2000 Pro combines a powerful 2,500A peak-output jump starter with a 16,000mAh battery, providing enough power to jump-start compatible vehicles without assistance from another driver.

It also doubles as a portable power bank for charging electronic devices, which could prove particularly useful if you're travelling somewhere remote and your phone is running low on power.

With its Black Friday price of $80.74, it's a practical addition to a winter emergency kit that could come in handy long after the colder months have passed.

Modern vehicles are packed with electronics that continuously track how different components are performing, but drivers often have very little access to this information.

OBD2 diagnostic scanners can connect to your vehicle's onboard diagnostic port and retrieve fault codes to better understand potential problems with your car.

For Android users, the TOPDON CarPal is an especially interesting starting point because it uses Bluetooth to send information directly to your smartphone.

Through the companion app, you can access vehicle health information and diagnostic trouble codes without taking the car to the repair shop for a checkup.

At $37.97 during TOPDON's Black Friday promotion, the CarPal A is also the most affordable diagnostic scanner in the lineup.

According to recent reports, drivers who enjoy carrying out their own maintenance might prefer something more advanced, such as the TOPDON AD600S or AD800BT2, which offer deeper diagnostic capabilities and additional service functions. Both models also benefit from free lifetime software updates.

Another interesting development in automotive diagnostics is the growing accessibility of thermal imaging technology, which can reveal unusual temperature differences that might indicate an underlying problem.

The TOPDON TC002C Duo connects directly to compatible USB-C Android smartphones, iPhones and tablets, essentially turning an everyday device into a portable thermal imaging camera.

It's useful for investigating potential overheating issues around vehicle components, but its applications extend well beyond automotive maintenance, as it can also identify heat-loss areas around your home.

The TC002C Duo is available for $229.89 during Black Friday, while TOPDON also offers standalone thermal cameras for customers who prefer dedicated equipment.

TOPDON’s Black Friday promotion runs from November 19 to November 30, 2026 and covers automotive equipment for casual drivers and professional mechanics alike.

If you've been considering putting together a winter emergency kit or investing in diagnostic equipment, it's worth exploring TOPDON's Black Friday offers before the promotional period ends.

El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface.
  • The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.
  • According to recent reports, A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface. He’s never seen anything like what’s been coming back for the past few months, as a super El Niño fuels record heat off the California coast. The marine heat wave is affecting wildlife and helping to juice the record-setting storms hitting the state at the start of the rainy season.

The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.

According to recent reports, A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface. Steric height—changes to sea levels driven by heat rather than melting ice—has reached the highest levels Rudnick has ever seen.

“I looked back at our data to make sure that I'm not making a mistake and it's correct—and it is,” Rudnick, who works at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, indicates.

It has been revealed that in Monterey Bay, a station recorded a temperature of 64.72 degrees Fahrenheit (18.18 degrees Celsius) at a depth of 200 feet below the water’s surface in late October, breaking previous records. Other data shows even hotter water in San Diego at the same depth: 77 degrees Fahrenheit, an anomaly of 21.3 degrees Fahrenheit above normal.

El Niño “is the biggest source of climate variability” off the California coast, Rudnick claims. The climate phenomenon is characterized by hotter-than-normal water in the eastern tropical Pacific and affects weather and oceans around the globe. His gliders have captured temperature anomalies across other events, including intense heat during the 2015–2016 super El Niño. But this year’s El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, and its impacts are equally supersized.

“It’s fair to say it’s off the charts,” he states.

Recent findings suggest that this year’s El Niño is adding heat to an already-simmering ocean. Since January 2025, coastal California waters have been hit by a massive heat wave, with temperatures in some places reaching 8 degrees Fahrenheit above average in August. Add in human-caused climate change—oceans off Southern California have warmed 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s alone—and it makes for unprecedented conditions now.

It has been revealed that “This is a bunch of things that have had to come together to make this even physically possible,” Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, indicates. “And even then, it's kind of astonishing.”.

Sources indicate that rudnick agrees. “The heat we get from El Niño stacking on top of the heat we already have, that’s the thing that makes this most unusual,” he notes.

Recent findings suggest that part of what’s driving the higher ocean temperatures and sea levels off California are what’s known as Kelvin waves. These slow, large waves transport warm water from west to east across the Pacific. They in turn push down the ocean’s thermocline, a transition layer into the deeper ocean where temperatures begin to decrease rapidly.

“It isn't like there's some heater in the deep ocean suddenly,” Swain indicates. “It's just that we've turned off the air conditioner and we're allowing the surface waters to warm.”.

Sources indicate that kelvin waves can also help to raise sea levels along the California coast by “keeping the water from moving physically offshore,” Swain indicates. While Kelvin waves are imperceptible to the average person, their impacts aren’t.

It has been revealed that californians have been living through several weeks of intense coastal flooding and major waves enhanced by these higher sea levels. San Francisco and the surrounding area are under a coastal flood advisory through Friday morning, and waves have reached over 30 feet (9 meters) in height and even set off seismographs. (Another storm is set to hit the Bay Area this weekend.) It’s also contributing to heavier rainfall, with locations from San Francisco to Burbank setting hourly rainfall records in recent days.

But the warmer water itself is also contributing to this temporary sea level rise, thanks to simple physics: Warmer water takes up more space, helping push up sea levels.

In a recent development, the warm water is driving weather even more unprecedented than the intense storms. On Tuesday, two rare twin waterspouts formed over San Francisco Bay, the result of cold storm air moving over unusually warm waters. These phenomena are generally seen off the coast of Florida or the Mediterranean—not in the usually frigid waters of the Pacific.

Recent findings suggest that “The air temperatures are somewhat winter-like right now, but the water ain't,” Swain says. “It’s an indicator that things aren’t as they usually are in this part of the world.”.

The Best Gifts for the Techie in Your Life (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • These are the major tech products that really got us amped up—many of which launched this year.
  • Updated November 2026: I've added the iPad Mini, Sonos Era 300, and the Lego Smart Play Star Wars Throne Room setup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Techy gizmos make great stocking stuffers or Secret Santa gifts for friends, family, or coworkers. In fact, we've collected them in our comprehensive list of the Best 40 Techy Gifts under $100—that should give you plenty to parse through for impulse buys and stocking stuffers.

But this list is not that. These are the major tech products that really got us amped up—many of which launched this year. They're more expensive than what you'd buy for an acquaintance, but if you're looking for a big reaction on Christmas morning from your kids, spouse, or significant other, one of these should do the trick.

Updated November 2026: I've added the iPad Mini, Sonos Era 300, and the Lego Smart Play Star Wars Throne Room setup.

Oura has a lock on the world of smart rings, and we've been loving the latest model, which came out this July. Because the Ring 5 is smaller and more comfortable than before, WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane claims she often forgets she's even wearing it. That's crucial for something you're supposed to wear at all times, including while sleeping or during workouts. It's billed as a “proactive” health and fitness platform, giving you data on everything from sleep patterns to predictive blood pressure signals. It's likely not worth upgrading from the previous version, but for the fitness and health nut in your life who doesn't own one yet, the Oura Ring 5 is the best smart ring you can buy.

It has been revealed that we already have smart speakers. We have iPads. We have digital photo frames (or, at least, your parents do). So, a dedicated device that serves merely as a digital calendar might seem superfluous. Maybe it is, but reviewer Nena Farrell absolutely swears by them. As someone with a busy family who struggles to sync our calendars, I get the appeal: a calendar on a larger screen in your kitchen or living room, visible to everyone who walks by, certainly sounds convenient. It's not just a list of events, either. It also has a meals page to blueprint and organize family dinners, plus tasks to keep everyone on top of chores. And this latest 15-inch model, the Skylight Calendar 2, is the best so far.

According to recent reports, it's not only our favorite Keychron keyboard—it's the best overall keyboard you can buy. Rolled out in early 2026, this mechanical keyboard has a mid-century modern vibe, made of wood and metal. The 75 percent layout gives you everything you'll likely need in a compact size, with all the usual Keychron features, such as hot-swappable switches, double-shot keycaps, and the usual excellent build quality. Unlike other mechanical keyboards you may have tried, this one is low-profile, which means the travel distance on each key isn't quite as long, and it's designed for typing first and foremost. It's a great office companion, and it'll be a smoother transition if you're coming from a more generic rubber-dome model like an Apple Magic Keyboard.

The iPhone Duo might be the talk of the town, but the latest iPad Mini is the more practical purchase. First of all, it doesn't require trading in the iPhone you're already familiar with to risk it on a first-generation product. It also isn't nearly as expensive if you already have a phone that you like. And what you get is easily the best small tablet money can buy. The deliciously vibrant OLED display is brighter and bigger than in the past, and if you opt for the nano-texture screen, it becomes the ultimate outdoor tablet. It might be a bit too expensive for a tablet of its size, but it just might be the ultimate travel companion for the right person.

Industry observers note that this Sonos speaker is built different, quite literally. It’s made specifically with Dolby Atmos spatial audio in mind, with six speaker drivers pointed in multiple directions to spread out sound like no other home speaker can. Outside of Atmos, it’s an excellent stereo speaker that sounds crisp and detailed, and can connect with Sonos soundbars to make a full surround sound setup. —Harry Rabinowitz.

Recent findings suggest that you know what they say: If it ain't broke, don't fix it. The Logitech MX Master 3S has long been the most popular productivity mouse you can buy, so expectations for its successor were high. Thankfully, the MX Master 4 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) delivers without rocking the boat too much. There's now haptic support in the thumb rest, and you can press here to activate the virtual Actions Ring. You can customize the ring in the Logi Options+ app to launch apps, open websites, insert symbols, or even type text—the options are nearly endless.

In a recent development, it might not be worth upgrading from the MX Master 3 or 3S, especially since the polling rate hasn't changed, but the MX Master 4 has taken the reins as the go-to wireless mouse for serious office workers. If you know someone who would appreciate a mouse that not only offers great ergonomic support but also feels extremely high-quality in the hand, look no further.

For more ideas for home office products that make great gifts, check out our comprehensive guide to the Best Work-from-Home Gear.

Recent findings suggest that whether it's the Rabbit R1 or Humane Pin, AI hardware has been a big flop so far. But this year, we finally started to see devices that are actually interesting and potentially useful. WIRED contributor Christopher Null tried out all the latest product category of AI notetaking devices, which can dictate, record, summarize, and translate seamlessly using large language models. Pocket was among the top recommendations. It magnetically attaches to the back of your phone and can even record phone calls without needing to keep it on speakerphone. Many AI notetakers require a paid subscription, while Pocket offers a substantial free option and only requires Pocket Pro as an upgrade for unlimited history.

With all the earbuds we review, you might think our audio experts are above something as common as AirPods. But Apple really nailed it this year with the AirPods Pro 3 (9/10, WIRED Recommends). It's been almost three years since Apple updated its noise-canceling earbuds, and the latest model adds a newly introduced ear tip design, supports real-time translation, and delivers vastly improved noise canceling and longer battery life. According to our testers, the earbuds last up to eight hours with noise canceling on, enough for more than a full day of work. All that makes this pair the best AirPods ever made.

Recent findings suggest that goPro has a latest premium camera, and it's one of the most expensive action cameras you can buy. But our camera expert and outdoors enthusiast, Scott Gilbertson, notes it's totally worth it. The new model, the GoPro Mission 1 Pro, has a larger 1-inch sensor than the Hero models, letting it shoot up to 8K at 60 fps. That might sound like overkill, but 8K lets you crop and zoom in on what you capture on your adventures while exporting to 4K without a significant hit to image quality (unless you're fortunate enough to own an 8K TV). Scott also praises the new slow-motion mode, shooting up to 4K at 240 fps—even when zoomed in. The older GoPro Hero 13 Black is still a great option if you want to save some money, but the Mission 1 Pro's upgrade in image quality is noteworthy for a camera this small.

The best espresso machines cost well over $1,000 and take up your entire kitchen counter. They aren't exactly very “giftable.” The Breville Bambino challenges that assumption. It's only $300, yet it has many of the same features as more expensive machines, such as a thermoblock for instant heating. Of course, as a smaller, budget option, it's missing some things, such as automatic milk frothing. But according to former WIRED reviewer, Matthew Korfhage, pairing the Bambino with a solid grinder gives you “beautiful cups with counter space to spare.” Who wouldn't want that?

According to recent reports, smart Play is Lego's next big move into adding some serious tech into its classic brick-building. Despite looking like standard Legos, each Smart Brick has a custom chip, light array, speaker, and a variety of sensors. You can probably imagine how all this tech plays out in a set as immersive as the Star Wars Throne Room Duel. If you want to experience the latest in the world of Lego, it doesn't get more cutting-edge than this (even if our reviewer found that the tech took some of the magic away).

💡 Key Takeaways
