Senior Director for Social Impact.

Your browser does not support the audio element.

In a recent development, this July, as the Railroad Fire spread through Washington overnight, Watch Duty sent its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert to its users. It started with a 911 dispatch buried in radio static — and a latest Gemini tool that caught it in seconds.

According to recent reports, A dedicated team of Google engineers and researchers spent six months embedded full-time with Watch Duty, a nonprofit wildfire alert app run by active and retired firefighters, dispatchers, and first responders. Through the Google.org Fellowship, they used more than 20,000 hours of past radio recordings to build a Gemini-powered tool that wipes out heavy static and translates specialized firefighting terminology into clean, searchable text. The system removes the added strain of deciphering noisy audio so volunteers can focus on verifying incidents and getting alerts out.

When a wildfire starts, minutes can decide whether people get out safely. Yet across much of the country, the first word of a fresh fire still travels over decades-old analog VHF radio, where engine noise, wind, static, and rapid-fire tactical jargon make it hard to hear what's happening. Watch Duty reporters monitor up to 20 feeds manually, making it a challenge to cut through the noise.

Across Watch Duty's network, the tool has:.

As a result of the collaboration between Google and Watch Duty, volunteer reporter satisfaction with radio transcription tools increased from 35.3% to 92.3%.

Industry observers note that the tool was also put to test during a live fire. In July 2026, a fast-moving wildfire — the Railroad Fire — ignited at night in Washington. When the first 911 dispatch went out over local fire radio, the Gemini-powered transcription tool transcribed it straight from the noisy radio audio and flagged it in under 30 seconds.

That head start gave Watch Duty's team the time they needed to verify the fire and push a Critical Alert—which breaks through do-not-disturb mode in urgent situations—helping residents evacuate before flames reached homes. It was the first time Watch Duty had ever sent a Critical Alert overnight, proving what faster detection means when communities are asleep and every minute counts.

The latest AI radio tool is the latest milestone in a deep, multi-year collaboration spanning Google's philanthropic, product, and research teams to help Watch Duty scale its life-saving mission across all 50 states.

When the next fire starts, the goal is simple: get people the warning they need while there's still time to act.

Don Bluth on the future of animation and AI: Thats definitely a road I dont want to travel on

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world.
  • It has been revealed that social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs.
  • In an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world. With movies like The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail, The Land Before Time, All Dogs Go to Heaven, and Anastasia, this American animator offered us realms of adventure, with plucky heroes as well as villains so fantastically frightening that we carry the thrill of it all with us decades later.

It has been revealed that social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs. Brisby being chased down by monstrous, roaring, ravenous cats. Now, for fans latest and old, filmmakers Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker offer Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There, a documentary that explores the life and work of the innovative animator through his own words.

In an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues. Together, they pursued animation not for the money but for the art and a deep desire to create something meaningful for future generations. Yet, when asked about his legacy, Bluth is quick to look back on the path that led him to his work.

He began by speaking of Winsor McCay, the father of American animation. In a wistful storyteller tone, Bluth recounted how a little boy witnessed the "magic" of the 1914 short film Gertie the Dinosaur, in which a pencil-sketched brontosaurus comes to life. This little boy was so inspired that he'd grow up to make his own animated short featuring a mouse named Mickey.

It has been revealed that that little boy, of course, was Walt Disney, who would go on to make 1937's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first animated feature film produced in the United States. That movie would go on to inspire a young Bluth, who'd direct his first animated feature in 1982 with The Secret of NIMH.

This path of inspiration to iconic art wasn't as direct a line as you might think.

Yes, Bluth scored a dream job, working at Disney Animation studio for 10 years on films like Sleeping Beauty, Robin Hood, and The Rescuers. But after Disney's death in 1966, Bluth and 17 other Disney animators feared the studio had lost their way, creatively.

He told Mashable he'd invite these artists to his home on weekends, where they'd draw together to develop innovative pitches for their corporate bosses. When they were shot down, Bluth — along with Gary Goldman and John Pomeroy — built their own manufacturer, Don Bluth Productions, to "see if we could do better than they were doing." For this, Bluth remembered, "We were called traitors.".

In a recent development, that's not how Bluth saw his team. "[These] wonderful people had the courage to leave their jobs and security and go out there and try and do something great," he mentioned, "not just to feed their egos, but something they felt helped them grow up. And they wanted to give back.".

It has been revealed that it was not an easy journey, as Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There details, revealing the highs and lows of Bluth's most beloved and worst-reviewed productions, as well as the wildly popular video game Dragon's Lair. In our interview, he spoke repeatedly about how the doc filled him with gratitude as he looked back for the filmmakers' interviews.

Recent findings suggest that to Mashable, he reflected, "What happened after so many movies, All Dogs Go to Heaven, American Tail, working with Steven Spielberg on both of those pictures, and George Lucas [on The Land Before Time], [it] became really, really obvious to us that we were doing the right thing [by] writing the right stories, and trying to make something that would move people's lives for the better — not just to pat our own backs and say, 'Look what we did.' [We were making] something that would help maybe children grow up and have some degree of morality about them. So then, that was our goal in everything.".

Industry observers note that in Somewhere Out There, the rise of computer animation — which Bluth refers to as "3D animation" — came as a devastating blow to the animator, who'd spent his life developing the skills of hand-drawn 2D animation. To this day, Bluth still advocates for the artistry of hand-drawn animation.

Industry observers note that "The way I look at this is animation in the 2D form is people, armed with a pencil in their hands, have to be able to draw," he explained, "and they also have to be able to act. And they have to have feelings about story.".

Sources indicate that to Bluth, CGI movies aren't animation. "3D animation is puppetry," he remarked, adding, "[With 3D animation,] you drop your pencil. You put your hands on a keyboard, and you make a wireframe puppet act.".

Bluth shared several of his complaints about the look of 3D animation, saying, "To me, it looks very plastic... The colors are muted, and they're trying to put shading in there, trying to look more like a live-action picture." He asked, "Why are we trying to get to a place which looks more real?" adding, "That isn't the purpose at all of 2D [animation]. The purpose is to take you to a magical world. 2D is trying to make audiences come to our own world.".

Noting the animation industry changed forever with the massive success of 1995's Toy Story, Bluth noted, "Toy Story [movies] were quite fun to watch, but they didn't make me feel anything very deep. And animation is intended to do that, particularly with Walt Disney pictures. Snow White, Bambi, [and] Pinocchio — those pictures did something to change the way you thought and help you grow up in a way that was really good. And they did it in such a beautiful way.".

Sources indicate that it was when Disney Studios, post-Walt, moved away from these tenets that Bluth and his colleagues set out on their own. He remarked, "We left the Disney Studio because it was leaving out the morality statements and leaving out all the beautiful colors and everything.".

In terms of what recent animated films impressed Bluth, he said, "I liked Klaus a lot," commending Sergio Pablos' inventive Christmas tale, which employs hand-drawn animation with a unique visual style.

It has been revealed that bluth also enjoyed Pete Docter's 2009 Pixar hit Up. "That was totally in 3D," he noted, "but it had a great story. For my taste, it went on too long. You know, the story was really about this couple promising each other they would go back to some place in their life, and she died. So, the man, true to the promise, tries to fulfill that [by taking their house on the journey]. So, I love that.".

Overall though, Bluth lamented, "Animation has become an advertisement for sugar cereal and whatever. There are more advertisements on animation than there are actually animated characters. The animated characters are just simply little puppets that jump up and down and tell one-line jokes. So, that's not good. Now, the last laugh is about to hit us like a tsunami; that is AI.".

Through the stories of Russian Jewish immigrant Fievel Mousekewitz, the widowed mother of four Mrs. Brisby, the orphaned brontosaurus Littlefoot, and rogue mutt Charlie B. Barkin, Bluth was striving to create stories that would inspire children to be good and creative, as Disney's movies had done for him. He doesn't see a future where AI can provide such mindful, moral guidance.

In a recent development, "It seems like AI is able to do wonderful, wonderful things," Bluth mused, "except AI is a machine, and it has no soul. It will borrow or steal, if you will, from everything that it knows, and give you what you ask for. But where's the creativity?".

"AI is a borrower," Bluth explained. "When you enter what you'd like to see, it searches all over and borrows it from other artists, puts it together. It indicates you on screen. Now, you can then make corrections. It can do all that, but it is still a machine. It doesn't ask you, 'Well, what is right and wrong? What is evil and good? What do you want me to say?' The machine can't do that.".

Industry observers note that he continued, "The only thing you can do is go back to human beings and say, 'Don't replace human beings with machines.' They're the ones who have a heart, who have a soul, and probably have a Creator. So, there's a bigger picture that's going on than just animation on a screen.".

"AI has no soul," Bluth concluded. "It hasn't a clue how to write anything. Everything that you're going to see on your screen has been stolen from other artists.".

According to recent reports, he allowed that some AI might be "stunningly beautiful," but "you'll find that it doesn't affect your heart the way you feel… They're not artists that are doing the AI. Many of them don't understand the art of acting or anything. So, what everything looks like in AI animation that I've seen, it all looks like slow motion, and it looks unreal. So, that's definitely a road I don't want to travel on.".

Industry observers note that "I read somewhere where someone remarked something that stuck in my head," he mused, paraphrasing Oscar Wilde's The Portrait of Dorian Gray. "There are many people who know the price of everything but the value of nothing. And I certainly hope that's not where we're going.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week I reported that Huawei was set to launch a new sub-brand called OSTA, with its first phone being an interesting wide-screen model called the OSTA O1 Pro. As of today, everything has been made official — and the OSTA O1 Pro is available to order now via the Huawei VMALL site in China.

As reliable Weibo tipsters suggested, the OSTA O1 Pro does indeed boast a unique wide form factor. Thanks to a newly uploaded spec sheet, we now know that it has a 6.39-inch display with a 120Hz refresh rate, starts at 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and is powered by the Kirin 9030S chipset – the same mid-range chip as the standard Huawei Pura 90.

The phone has a 7,000mAh battery, with support for 66W SuperCharge and 5W wired reverse charging, as well as 50W wireless charging when using a compatible charger. As for the cameras, the OSTA O1 Pro has a 200MP main shooter paired with a 50MP telephoto lens. There doesn't seem to be a dedicated ultra-wide or macro lens present. There is, however, a 50MP selfie camera on the front of the phone.

Industry observers note that the OSTA O1 Pro is available in three colours: Starry Night Black, Nebula White, and Starlight Purple (though the latter is only offered in 16GB+512GB and 16GB+1TB configurations). Prices start at 5699 CNY for the most basic model, which comes to roughly $855 or £650.

Recent findings suggest that the OSTA O1 Pro would be a pretty unexceptional mid-range phone, were it not for that unique wide-screen format. It almost looks like an iPhone Air, but fatter and more... compressed. That's not a bad thing either, as I think wider formats like this definitely have a place.

The popularity of the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 (which is similarly stout) reveals that Android owners are certainly interested in trying form factors that are a bit more out there than the usual candy bar shape. The design of the OSTA O1 Pro also just looks like it would be very comfortable in the hands and fit comfortably in most pockets.

Wider aspect ratios have advantages when it comes to multitasking too, as they make it easier to view multiple windows side by side when using the phone horizontally.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

The big question is whether the OSTA O1 Pro will make it to the West in any official capacity and, sadly, I don't think it's likely. Huawei pulled out of the US market following a US government ban in 2022 and has largely stopped selling its handsets in the UK as well. The only phones right now listed on the Huawei UK site are the Mate XT Ultimate Design and Mate X6 foldable, neither of which is actually available to buy on the store.

That stated, we might still see other manufacturers come out with their own wide-screen model – especially if the OSTA O1 Pro proves popular with Chinese consumers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after rapidly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked.
  • Sources indicate that the MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player.
  • In a recent development, while the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after rapidly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

Sources indicate that the MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

And, yeah, they live up to the hype.

In a recent development, while the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

In a recent development, as for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

Industry observers note that for $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

It has been revealed that sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

iOS 27.3 Apple Intelligence, Siri AI usage limits: What to know

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • All good things must come to an end implement usage limits.
  • Just a few months after Apple finally debuted the long-awaited Siri AI, its upgraded voice assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, the organization will now implement daily usage limits.
  • Basically, if a user hits those limits, they will need to upgrade their paid iCloud+ account or wait for the daily limits to reset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All good things must come to an end implement usage limits.

Just a few months after Apple finally debuted the long-awaited Siri AI, its upgraded voice assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, the organization will now implement daily usage limits. These new restrictions will be implemented along with the launch of iOS 27.3.

What does this mean? Basically, if a user hits those limits, they will need to upgrade their paid iCloud+ account or wait for the daily limits to reset. However, not every Siri AI request counts towards people' daily limits.

So, what counts towards your daily Siri AI limits? How much does it cost to upgrade? Lets break down everything you need to know about the new Siri AI usage limits.

According to Apple, "Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are available for free for people with a supported device set to a supported language." However, "some features rely on powerful server models and have limits.".

Apple claims the following features will have daily usage limits:.

Images: Intelligent Photo Editing Tools, which include Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing, as well as Image Playground.

Workflows and automation: AFM Cloud and AFM Cloud Pro models in Shortcuts.

Third-party apps that use Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute.

Apple has not published exactly what the daily usage limits are for Apple Intelligence or Siri AI. The manufacturer's Support page simply describes it as a "generous daily usage limit.".

According to recent reports, notably, each of those above categories has its own unique daily usage limits. These are not shared between those features, which means a user can hit the daily limit for one but not the others.

Daily usage limits are connected at the Apple account level and are implemented across all Apple devices, including iOS devices, Mac, and Apple TV.

When a user reaches their daily limit, they will receive a prompt after making a request that counts towards those limits. Advanced requests are paused until the daily limit resets or the user upgrades to an iCloud+ plan.

Industry observers note that "Daily Request Limit Reached," the prompt reads on iOS. "You can continue with basic requests.".

The prompt also includes a button to upgrade to an iCloud+ strategy to increase those daily limits.

Industry observers note that as previously mentioned, Apple isn't sharing exactly what those Apple Intelligence and Siri AI limits are. However, they have shared just how many times those "generous" limits are increased when upgrading to an iCloud+ initiative.

Industry observers note that here's an outline of what you get with each iCloud+ proposal: The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

200GB: $2.99 per month – Up to 2x daily usage limit.

2TB: $9.99 per month – Up to 5x daily usage limit.

6TB: $29.99 per month – Up to 10x daily usage limit.

12TB: $59.99 per month – Up to 20x daily usage limit.

The 50GB iCloud+ initiative, which Apple sells for $0.99 per month, does not include any increase in daily usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.

Apple indicates that all feature categories will have their daily limits reset at approximately midnight in the user's current time zone.

Recent findings suggest that according to Apple, users who are travelling internationally will have their limits reset "around midnight in the central time zone of the country or region of your Apple Account." Users who share an iCloud+ strategy with a Family Sharing group will see their limits reset at around midnight of the time zone of the iCloud+ plan purchaser. Users who aren't signed into their Apple Account will see their limits reset around 24 hours after they first used that feature category that day.

Unused limits from the previous day do not roll over.

According to recent reports, starting with iOS 27.3, Siri AI will also receive limits for certain "advanced" tasks. Apple notes that basic tasks will continue to be unlimited and will work even when the daily usage limits for advanced tasks are reached.

You may be wondering what a "basic" task is and what is an "advanced" task, the latter of which will have daily usage limits.

Apple provided the following examples as a basic task, which people will be able to utilize without limits:.

"Set a timer for three minutes.".

"Text Mark that Annika's party is at 123 Main Street.”.

As for advanced tasks, Apple provides these examples:.

"Text Mark the address for Annika's party, and tell him what time we need to leave from home to make it on time.".

"Add a summary of my San Francisco trip note to this email draft.".

Based on those examples, it appears advanced tasks involve multi-step requests that require server-side processing.

Recent findings suggest that beyond Apple's official published examples, Apple leaker pdfu has uncovered Apple's more detailed instructions given to Siri AI telling the assistant how to decide if a user has reached their limits for advanced tasks. In an X post, the leaker explained Siri will take limits into account if a user request:.

uses information from one app, from what is on screen or from a message, in a different app, or needs a result from one step used in a different step or app (such as a looked-up fact typed into a field).

contains two or more separate asks in one sentence, even in the same app (extra details of one action, such as a cc or a time, are still one ask).

asks about or summarizes the content of a photo, a camera view or an attachment (editing, searching and albums are fine).

deletes, archives, junks, moves, marks or changes a set (all, every, these or a whole category) of the user’s emails, notes, reminders, messages, photos, files, contacts or events.

sets a device action or a notification to run on a time or trigger (not alarms, timers, reminders or calendar events), notifies someone when a person arrives or leaves, or builds or edits a Shortcut or automation.

is deep research or a multi-step task done on the user’s behalf.

asks you to compose or create new content (a story, poem, essay, plan, recipe, image, or an email or message from a topic rather than wording the user gives), or to rewrite in a tone other than friendly, professional or concise.

A user asking a third-party AI assistant like ChatGPT for an advanced request is never limited, even if a user reaches their daily usage limit for the day.

According to pdfu, tasks like "proofreading, rewriting in a friendly, professional or concise tone, summaries as key points, a list or a table, typing or sending wording the user gives, a single direct operation in any app, even when Siri must look the target up first (the closest bakery, my cousin), 'this' or 'that' within its own app, running a Shortcut by name, a reminder for yourself by time or place, Find My, sharing your ETA or location, and all your home accessories (lights, doors, locks), alarms, timers or device settings" all fall under basic tasks.

Recent findings suggest that so far, Apple hasn't released much more on these latest daily usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. Hopefully, before iOS 27.3 comes out, Apple provides owners with more specific information regarding what does and doesn't count towards their daily usage limits.

#2271. Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again

Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set upcoming limits on screenshots.
  • Whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers.
  • Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set upcoming limits on screenshots. The tech giant will prevent screenshotting in its iOS 27 app and “when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android,” Signal President Meredith Whittaker wrote in a blog post Friday.

Whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers. These features observe what’s on a user’s screen as context for completing requests.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.

“Your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” Whittaker said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

Signal also blocked screenshots last year in response to Microsoft’s controversial Recall AI feature, which could capture screenshots of Signal chats on devices running Windows 11.

Signal’s move is another reminder of how Substantial Tech’s AI strategy trickles downstream. As AI features have moved from services external to the OS (like chatbots from OpenAI or Anthropic) to further inside of it, third-party apps have to adapt to conditions that undermine their hard-won privacy infrastructure.

Also: How I use Meta Muse safely to stretch my AI budget – and what I never let it do.

In a recent development, just last week, researchers at Google DeepMind used AI agents to formally verify Signal’s code, building on Signal’s own work to essentially prove the app’s encryption works. That’s a high bar for a security guarantee within the app, but it becomes meaningless if an agent can simply grab messages off a screen.

Samsung is reportedly working on its own agent, Galaxy Claw, and Apple is developing a rival for Claude and ChatGPT as well.

Whittaker noted Signal’s screenshot restriction isn’t perfect, saying that AI agents can still access app data through other means, “such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.” Earlier this week, a Reuters investigation supported by Signal and the AI Now Institute found that Meta’s Muse AI agent was using permissions from its initial setup in unexpected ways to access apps and data that a user had not explicitly connected it to.

Signal noted its protections don’t currently work on MacOS.

“It is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” she added. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience.”.

If you’d still like to take screenshots, you can simply disable the setting, though Signal’s announcement strongly advised against it.

“Doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees,” Whittaker noted.

  • Industry observers note that the Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be.
  • Recent findings suggest that last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery enhancement detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

Industry observers note that the Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

Recent findings suggest that last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery enhancement detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a fresh update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain issues caused by something other than RAM.

Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the firm’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

It has been revealed that the post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded issues have pushed production back, and users are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese Latest Year.

In an act of good faith, Clicks indicates it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

Sources indicate that A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

I've been testing smart bird feeders for more than two years in my own backyard, and Birdfy has been—and still is—the brand I trust and recommend most. These feeders are well-made, reliable, and reasonably priced. The brand's app is also excellent; it's easy to navigate and use without shelling out for an additional subscription. Better still, Birdfy just rolled out free lifetime AI ID (which is quite decent) with any bird feeder, including the lowest-priced models. If you don't want to gift a traditional feeder, you might consider Birdfy's smart birdbath and nesting box, each of which comes equipped with the same high-quality camera(s).

Below are the models I've tested—in some cases for years—and recommend, including a couple I personally plan to buy as gifts this year.

Sources indicate that WIRED first reviewed this feeder in 2022. Back then we loved the concept, but felt its AI ID didn't quite cut it. Birdfy has come a long way since then on the AI front. The feeder body is largely the same, but the app and AI ID (now free) are both much improved, offering a seamless and user-friendly experience that makes it easy to sort through which birds visited that day. This once-pricey feeder is now at the lowest price I have ever seen for the version without the solar panel. The 5200-mAh rechargeable battery lasts a few weeks, but I think it's convenient to not have to bring it in to charge, if you want to spring for the extra $20 for that solar panel.

According to recent reports, birdfy's “beginner” model, this unit is basically a gravity pet feeder with a camera on the side. All you need to do is snap three pieces together, charge the camera, and pair it to the Birdfy app. If you know anyone who loves birds but is intimidated by the thought of having to set up and calibrate a smart bird feeder, this could be the perfect gift for them. However, note that my test unit keeps losing its lid on windy days, and there's no roof to keep the seed from getting wet on rainy days, so it's probably best for summer use. I also just discovered that Walmart carries an exclusive periwinkle color that looks lovely.

Birdfy's Metal 2 4K is the brand's flagship release for this year, with Ultra 4K resolution and dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi connection. The metal body claims to resist squirrels, and the muted green color is a welcome change from Birdfy's usual bright plastics. As was the case with the brand's previous flagship, the Feeder 2 Pro, I had some significant connection problems with the Metal 2 4K. This kept it from being a top pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, but the model is still worth a mention here due to its combination of features and build quality, as well as Birdfy's excellent customer service if something does go wrong.

Sources indicate that smart bird feeders aren't always the most aesthetically pleasing thing you could put in your yard, but Birdfy's 2K bamboo model was the first smart feeder I've ever had that actually garnered compliments. The natural wood and waterfall-style black roof complement any landscaping or exterior decor, and the camera and overall setup ran flawlessly for me during my months of testing. Just make sure you apply varnish or urethane regularly to the bamboo, as the finish on mine peeled after only two months in mild weather.

Recent findings suggest that this interesting product pairs a plastic birdbath (on an optional metal stand) with a solar-powered camera, so you can keep an eye on visiting birds without having to deal with seed mess. When I first tested it, I was worried birds would splash water on the camera lens, but the most popular activity at the bath is by far drinking the water (birds, raccoons, squirrels … anything passing by). I don't love that the basin grows algae promptly and the pump clogs easily, but this is otherwise a very well-made item—it's been in my yard for a year and a half through every season, and while the plastic is starting to fade a bit, it's still going strong.

Though I do love a smart bird feeder, Birdfy's Nest Duo is the absolute zenith of bird-watching for me. A black-capped chickadee moved in, laid eggs, and raised chicks (detailed here), and the cameras and app on the Nest stayed working, giving me 24-hour updates with interior night vision and views of the entry hole's exterior to see who was coming and going. A remote control on a 10-foot-long cord lets you reset or charge the camera without bothering the birds (though the auxiliary solar panel worked great for me). Note, however, that the black waterfall-style roof and lack of ventilation do pose a risk of overheating any young birds; during a May heat wave, I had to affix an umbrella and ice packs to the box, but the interior thermometer and hygrometer did a great job keeping me abreast of changing conditions.

Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud.
  • Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.
  • Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud.

Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she claims.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she states.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she claims.

Credit scores are "backward looking" says Funmi Olufunwa.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

According to recent reports, "A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she claims.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a manufacturer called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart mentioned in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more rapidly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk.".

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, states Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination.".

Upstart notes it is tackling that glitch.

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the firm said in a statement.

Evangeline Atkinson (left) and Laura Mills co-founders of Noggin HQ.

Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.

Recent findings suggest that "I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a Â£30-a-month phone contract, and they mentioned no," she recalls.

It has been revealed that "When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the massive three credit reference agencies.".

That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.

In a recent development, their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.

The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.

Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".

"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics.".

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August.

Perhaps conscious of change, the massive three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian confirmed a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting consumers check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax released a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it states uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion revealed it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".

As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.

"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there.".

Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.

Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.

"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.

"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," notes Olufunwa.

#2262. Andrey Zvyagintsev believes filmmakers know what the audience wants — not executives

Andrey Zvyagintsev believes filmmakers know what the audience wants — not executives

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The director of Minotaur indicates there is no politics in Russia.
  • The director of Minotaur notes there is no politics in Russia.
  • In a recent development, the year is 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The director of Minotaur indicates there is no politics in Russia.

The director of Minotaur notes there is no politics in Russia.

In a recent development, the year is 2022. Vladimir Putin has revealed the military draft. In Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, set in the fictional town of Krasoborsk, a quietly unhappy couple, called Gleb and Galina, carry on with their lives, or try to, geopolitics notwithstanding. For Galina, carrying on means an affair, which we deduce from a scene of her texting with a faint smile, her face lit in the dark by the light of her phone. (Minotaur is a remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film The Unfaithful Wife, whose title gives the plot away more readily than Zvyagintsev’s.).

Meanwhile, Gleb runs a kind of private contracting concern and is soon asked to scare up military recruits to meet a quota. At this point, the domestic noir and the workplace drama merge to dramatic, devastating, and darkly funny effects.

According to recent reports, in Minotaur, as in his five other features, Zvyagintsev has the camera moving seemingly objectively, almost omnisciently, putting the characters in their context. Occasionally they appear rather small, especially when set against the epic scale of their mythic and biblical fates. That the environment shapes the person seems to be a recurring revelation across all six of his staggering films. Minotaur, too, opens with a natural landscape of the arboreal kind and ends with another, different landscape, of clouds. In the middle is a movie about people trying to make sense of the landscapes they find themselves in, of the social, moral, relational variety.

According to recent reports, zvyagintsev has some experience with finding oneself in incomprehensible landscapes. After receiving Russia’s Sputnik V covid-19 vaccine during the pandemic, he fell ill, and later learned about the invasion of Ukraine while recovering from a medical coma in Germany. He subsequently chose not to return home, moving to France.

At the Cannes Film Festival in May, Minotaur won the second-highest honor. In his acceptance speech, Zvyagintsev spoke about the war, saying: “The only person who can stop this butchery is the President of the Russian Federation. Put an end to this carnage. The whole world is waiting for it.” While he resists the identity of exile, in September the Russian government designated him a “foreign agent.”.

Zvyagintsev returned this year to the Latest York Film Festival, where he last visited with his 2014 film Leviathan, which won a Golden Globe and was nominated for an Oscar. His debut in 2003, The Return, won a top prize at Venice International Film Festival, after which he was invited to meet Putin, an account of which appears in his forthcoming book. Out of his six films, four have won prestigious prizes at Cannes, including Elena and Loveless.

Industry observers note that we discussed the three years he spent cleaning the streets of Moscow in the early 1990s, his status as a Russian immigrant in France now, and how he captures that great Chekhovian instinct: that life is wretched, but what can we do, we must go on living. Zvyagintsev spoke to The Verge through a translator from Los Angeles.

I understand you went from cleaning streets to making commercials. What happened in between?

According to recent reports, it kind of happened almost at the same time, because I was cleaning the streets to be able to live in Moscow. From 1990 to 1993, I was cleaning the streets. And then I was going to the Museum of Cinema and watching a movie every single day. Those were my formative years, when I learned a lot about cinema.

I had been living in a huge communal flat, free accommodation in a beautiful historic mansion in central Moscow. It was a really massive apartment, and there were three street cleaners, including me, that lived there. In 1993, I was forced to leave the apartment after someone from the local housing administration decided to take it over. The two others had families, so they decided that if someone was supposed to move, it was going to be me, since I was single.

I was offered alternative accommodation, but realized that the only reason I had continued working as a street sweeper was to keep that particular apartment.

Industry observers note that so the first night when I had to leave the apartment, I left it fast without an actual blueprint. I had to spend the night inside a truck that was abandoned and that was parked in the street.

I got a fresh job as a guard, as a night guard at a kindergarten where I also ate leftover food from the children’s meals.

It has been revealed that after the first day, I called my friend who was working in commercials and doing music videos. I asked him to help with a job, because I was sure I was able to shoot commercials. After the first commercial, I met some producers who liked my work, and then I started shooting commercials on the regular and working as a freelance for some time. One of those commercials was noticed by a producer from a TV channel called REN TV, who was shooting a bunch of TV series at the time. His name was Dmitry Lesnevsky and he asked me whether I wanted to shoot movies, and I mentioned it was my dream. And then Dmitry presented me with 15 scripts of choice, and I shot three episodes of a television series called The Black Room for this channel, each 25 minutes long.

We were army friends. He was a close friend from the army. He was a cinema mechanic. He was starting movies for the soldiers when they were in the army. They had a theater, and I was in the music ensemble in the army. He was also an actor.

You had an adverse reaction to a covid vaccine. You were ill for a long time. You nearly died. You moved, and eventually settled in France. You’ve remarked you can’t know how that experience changed you as a filmmaker, but I’m curious if you know how that experience changed you as a person.

I got sick in Russia. I was in a coma for 40 days in Germany. I had a major problem with my lungs, a bacteria called klebsiella found its way there. They thought that they would need a lung transplant. Fortunately, the Germans were able to operate, and the transplant was not needed. I moved to France a year later after the coma.

What was the biggest change for me was the rhythm of life. I understood that you cannot lose time, so I’m trying to do things in a much more dynamic manner, and not leave things for later because we don’t know if this later exists. So that that’s the biggest change, really, just seeing life as something that passes by swiftly.

You are a vocal opponent of the current Russian government. Do you consider yourself to be in political exile?

I am not in political exile. I did not have that status, and I never applied for it because I don’t see any necessity for that. I consider myself an immigrant. I’ve been living away from my native country for almost five years, but I did not leave on purpose. I was already in Europe when the war happened. There is a term in Russian, called nevozvrashchenets, which means a person who does not come back, someone who has left their home country and has not returned, particularly for political reasons. I was in the clinic in Germany and then in France when the war started, and I realized that I could not go back to the country that is at war.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve said you are not political, but your movies seem overtly political, to me. You’ve also said that the job of an artist is to reflect reality. You don’t think you’re political, but your job is to reflect reality, and we are living at a time when politics is dominant. How do you reconcile all this?

Recent findings suggest that it’s very simple to reconcile. It’s just that the politics barges into our lives, and we have to reflect what’s going on in the world. You become a witness of what’s going on beyond your window, what’s going on to the environment, to the world around you, to the world close to you. It just so happens that the politics dominate our lives. We are witnessing historical events that we cannot not reflect in the movies.

Industry observers note that “There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews… This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power”.

In a recent development, when I say I’m not a political animal, I mean that I have no way of influencing the political process in my country, especially while the war is going on. There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews, you know, left, right, Democrats, Republicans. This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power.

It feels more like domination in the way Foucault meant it.

Yes. It’s not even that there is only one party that dominates. It’s that no one even questions it, and no one even tries to struggle. It’s kind of a totalitarian regime at this time.

In a recent development, let’s talk Minotaur. I believe you mentioned you wanted to adapt Ingrid Bergman first, but when that didn’t go, you asked your producers for other available properties and they sent you a list. You also said you asked for marital dramas from the ’60s and ’70s specifically. Why?

In a recent development, I wanted to do a remake of a movie that would have three or four main characters, not a lot of different locations, that would be a little more compact, because there was a certain budget consideration. The films that I had previously considered, the scripts I considered, were more expensive, and so I was not able to get any of them going.

And that’s when I asked for the list from my friend who is French, and he gave me a list of French films. If I had an Italian friend, those would have been Italian movies.

Industry observers note that I asked him for the best films from the ’60s and ’70s because it’s far away enough for us, those were probably the films that were a little bit more forgotten by the public, or a latest generation of the public maybe hasn’t seen them. And that’s how I discovered Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife.

You also stated that something about the Chabrol did not work for you, and that’s what gave you the inspiration to want to remake it.

It has been revealed that I wouldn’t formulate it as something not working, but I would rather say that he made a kind of a formal choice when it comes to the office life of the main character. Chabrol concentrates more on the crime plot and the love triangle [than the office life], which is totally his right.

It has been revealed that and I thought it was something that I would like to fill in. In 2022, the war was going on, and then in September they started the partial mobilization in Russia, and so this plot kind of just barged into our movie, and filled out that space that was empty previously.

According to recent reports, your movies are full of scenes Hollywood executives would ask to cut. I am thinking of the ending of Minotaur, with the clouds, or The Banishment, which ends with women collecting hay and they are singing. What is the effect of these moments in your movies?

It would be impossible to cut out those moments.

What are they doing in the movie?

Recent findings suggest that when you say that Hollywood execs would probably like to cut that stuff out, the viewers, including viewers in Hollywood, really like the clouds [that Minotaur ends on], for example, and they even tell me that the sequence could have been longer. So I want to tell you that the execs do not know what the viewers want because when the viewer goes to the cinema, he kind of goes to sleep and then he watches a dream. And as long as this dream is aesthetically pleasing and harmonious and beautiful, that’s what the viewers should be watching, and no one should cut that out.

It has been revealed that this is the key conflict between the producer and the creator. The producer does not trust the creator to know what the audience wants, but the creator knows. And so, if the producer is so sure of himself, he should write a script himself.

You published a book about the making of your third film, Elena. I understand you’re working on a second book. What can you tell us about this project? Will it include advice to young filmmakers?

The whole book, in a way, will be an advice to younger filmmakers, or people who love movies, because it will be a very detailed account of the six films that I have released so far, six conversations with one of the best cinema critics writing in Russian, Anton Dolin.

Would you ever work in another language apart from Russian or with Netflix?

Yes, I am open. In fact, I have a script in English. Two even.

Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a upcoming update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t at the moment provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

Fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Users who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the fresh toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:.

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a fresh toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq.

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:.

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

It’s good to see that customers can manually disable the fresh privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise key questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

In a recent development, apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing consumers to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

What do you think of Signal’s latest move? Let us know in the comments.

Jolly, the mascot of Meta’s Muse AI agent.

In a recent development, meta employees found Muse, the company’s AI agent, reading encrypted messages and making up purchases. It also sent them chats that seemed meant for other people. That is according to more than two dozen internal posts reviewed by Reuters’ Katie Paul, published on Wednesday.

Staff raised concerns that Muse could be mixing up conversations between accounts and exposing private data, the posts showed. Muse has passed 10 million downloads since its September launch. Meta expects it to generate billions of dollars, Reuters reported.

In one post, an employee mentioned Muse added an unprompted line to a chat about fishing weather.

“BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57,” the message read.

Another employee said Muse reminded her to reply to her sister on Signal, the encrypted messaging app.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” she wrote.

Sources indicate that A colleague found that Muse had permission by default to read push notifications on Android phones. One employee stated Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb stay without permission. Another said it offered to message a seller about a coffee table in what was “not my conversation”.

Reuters could not establish whether Muse was showing owners other people’s data or making it up. In early November, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team gave the internal feedback group an explanation. Built-in prompts push the agent to engage users between sessions, and it appeared to hallucinate messages in response.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, reuters worked with Signal staff and the AI Now Institute to repeat the Signal access. On an Android phone, Muse read messages through its notification permission. On a Mac, it used Apple’s accessibility and screenshot tools. The same requests failed on an iPhone.

Sources indicate that apple said its accessibility tools were built for people with disabilities. An Apple revision this week closed that route on Macs, Reuters reported. It also added a latest set of permissions for agents. In October, Apple tightened Full Disk Access because of AI agents. A journalist had said Muse read the messages on his Mac. Meta denied that claim at the time.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts called the examples “isolated incidents” and said Muse reaches other apps only through permissions consumers explicitly grant, Reuters reported. Many of the suspected account mix-ups were hallucinations that Meta had already fixed, he said. He declined to say how many there were.

Meta gave TechCrunch a further statement on Thursday.

“Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere,” a Meta spokesperson noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a time when Anthropic is vacuuming up stock market money, the AI organization has made a pretty grandiose claim about its Claude chatbot's scientific capabilities.

The San Francisco-based artificial intelligence firm published a lengthy blog post this week claiming that its Claude Fable 5.2 model had made some progress on figuring out two long-standing mysteries surrounding black holes. The post goes into an incredible amount of scientific detail that might fly over your head (as much of it did mine), but I'll try my best to summarize it in plain English.

In a recent development, according to Anthropic, the first conundrum Claude was able to solve involved the concept of heating up a hypothetical universe. When the universe reaches a certain temperature, it would form a black hole through a sudden "phase transition," as initially described by Stephen Hawking and Don Page in 1983. Hawking and Page's findings concerned only a vast universe described by general relativity, while this theoretical universe is much smaller and might work differently.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

It has been revealed that it turns out, as Claude found, that the phase transition is also abrupt in a smaller universe. As Anthropic explained, this implies that "black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.".

As for the second finding, it revolves around another theoretical universe made up of two dimensions instead of three. In this universe, physicists have spent years trying to figure out how heavy the lightest possible black hole could be using a technique called "bootstrapping," in which the ceiling for the lightest black hole gets lowered each time a theory breaks it. Anthropic claimed that Claude Fable 5.2 was able to notice a pattern that physicists had missed in their calculations and use it to "calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered.".

As Anthropic was quick to point out in the blog post, these findings do not apply to our universe or have any practical application but could give us an idea of how relativity and quantum mechanics work together. It's also worth noting that these findings were released alongside Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO, AKA a time when Anthropic wants as much public money as possible.

Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his latest record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t.
  • Sources indicate that “I do the same I kind of always do.
  • On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘I always look for the newest machines.’.

According to recent reports, if you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his latest record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge.

Sources indicate that “I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he says. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.”.

On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4. “It’s just so powerful, and it sounds so big,” he says. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to newly introduced and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “Shut It Down,” “1+1+1,” and “Ycore.”.

Industry observers note that “The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something new that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha states. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that he looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can, Amon Düül, and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft. He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments.

But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he claims, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.”.

Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services.

Palo Alto Networks buys AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5bn in stock

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn.
  • Applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers.
  • “Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” noted Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Palo Alto Networks’ office in Singapore.

Sources indicate that palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn. The startup helps companies train and run their own versions of open-weight AI models. Palo Alto revealed the deal on Wednesday, minutes after The Wall Street Journal’s Kate Clark reported it.

Applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers. Earlier this month it raised $350m at a $3.25bn valuation, the Journal reported. It also stated it had reached $100m in run-rate revenue. Its co-founder and chief executive, Yash Patil, will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer when the deal closes. The deal still needs regulatory clearance and should close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” noted Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.

Open-weight models let owners download and change the weights, the numbers that set how a model behaves. Palo Alto said no large provider offers them securely today. It intends to let companies train, adapt and run them in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. Applied Compute will keep serving its own customers, and Palo Alto will sell the platform to its own base.

Arora told the Journal the deal means “venturing outside of cybersecurity”. On the earnings call, he remarked open-weight models now carry more than 60% of token traffic. A year ago it was under 5%.

“If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do,” Arora mentioned on the call.

Palo Alto told analysts it expects the deal to add more than $1bn in annual recurring revenue by fiscal 2029. It intends to build more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity. Capital spending on that will stay under $3bn through fiscal 2030, it said.

Arora also addressed whether Applied Compute’s team will stay. Its staff have “millions of reasons” to stay for the next three to four years, he wrote on X. They will keep their offices and, for the most part, their independence.

The deal came with Palo Alto’s fiscal first-quarter results. Revenue rose 39% to $3.44bn in the three months to 31 October. Annual recurring revenue from its next-generation security business rose 66% to $9.73bn. Net income was $482m, up from $334m a year earlier.

Palo Alto raised its forecasts for the year. It now expects revenue of $14.52bn to $14.57bn. It sees adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 a share.

On the call, Arora linked part of that demand to the recent run of outages. He blamed them partly on IT teams rushing to patch AI-found flaws. He has argued before that AI prices must fall for the technology to take off. He has also called slowing AI down unrealistic.

Utah sues Stake four days after the site added the state to its blocked list

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022.
  • Sources indicate that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out.
  • Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

Sources indicate that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner said access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint states.

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

The central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

The complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

Utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the manufacturer to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

Recent findings suggest that utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

Other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

Recent findings suggest that the Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the tech giant did not answer a request for comment on the suit.
